title: The ambrosial Name
hook: sukhmanee sukh amrit prabh naam: this jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name (Sukhmani 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhaanaa, and your line: perfect, underneath. A week ends today. The Guru cleared the eyes; we saw within and without, drisat, learned to see freshly, then met the perfect One. Today, the line the whole bani is named for. Day five hundred thirty-two.

Plenty of books take their title from one line buried inside them. You're reading along, and there on an ordinary page is the phrase from the cover, and suddenly the whole book makes a little more sense. Sukhmani has a line like that. It isn't saved for the end. It's planted near the very beginning, and the bani's name comes from it. As Sukhmani closes, we turn back to it: the ambrosial Name.
screen: `A TITLE ON AN ORDINARY PAGE.` → `PLANTED NEAR THE BEGINNING.` → `THE AMBROSIAL NAME.`

segments.voice: The line comes right after Sukhmani's first stanza, marked rahao, which means pause: the place in a hymn where you stop and take in the center. In paraphrase: Sukhmani, the jewel of peace, is the ambrosial Name of God; it rests in the minds of the devotees. Start with the name of the bani. Sukh is peace, ease, happiness. Mani can be read as a jewel, so Sukhmani is often called the jewel of peace; some also hear man, the mind, in it, peace of mind. Either way, the line tells you what that jewel actually is. It isn't the poem. It's the Name. Then amrit. Amrit is the nectar of immortality in old Indian stories, the drink of the gods. In Gurbani, amrit comes up again and again: the amrit vela before dawn, the amrit of the Name, and the amrit Sikhs receive at initiation. It means what gives true life, sweet and undying. And the last phrase: bhagat janaa kai man bisraam. Bisraam is rest, a place to stop and lay down a load, like a traveler's inn. The Name is where the devotee's mind comes to rest. One way to read Sukhmani, then: all twenty-four ashtpadis, with their warnings and their stories, their stillness and their praise, unpack this one line. Pride and humility, wealth and kindness, the wanderer and the beggar, the cleared eyes: each was a way into the same rest. Sukhmani's peace is not a mood. It's a Name, remembered.
screen: `RAHAO: THE PAUSE AT THE CENTER.` · `SUKHMANI: THE JEWEL OF PEACE.` · `AMRIT: WHAT GIVES TRUE LIFE.` · `BISRAAM: WHERE THE MIND RESTS.` · then, large: `THE NAME IS PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in peace for one minute, and then a second. Sit comfortably and let the body grow heavy. With each breath, imagine setting down a load, the way a traveler sets down a bag at an inn. One load per breath: a worry, a task, a conversation. If you pray, you can let the Name, Waheguru, be the place where you set each one down. If you don't, let the breath itself be the resting place. The bell holds the time.
Amrit, the nectar of immortality: Sukhmani's rahao line says the jewel of peace is God's amrit Name, the place where the devotee's mind finds bisraam, rest.
Your line: the name is peace. Today, at one stressful moment, pause and set down one load on a single breath. Day five hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib pause at its rahao line, which calls the jewel of peace God's ambrosial Name, resting in the minds of devotees.

fork.setup: you've read all twenty-four ashtpadis. according to the rahao line, what is Sukhmani's jewel of peace?
fork.reveal: the line says the jewel of peace is the amrit Name of God, resting in the minds of the devotees.

original.note: Gurmukhi: amrit, nectar of immortality; in Gurbani, what gives true, undying life.

trapdoor: what you thought: the ambrosial Name is a sweet way to say God's name.
what it means: Sukhmani's jewel of peace is the Name itself, where the mind finally rests.
what a scholar hears: the line is Sukhmani's rahao, placed after the first stanza; in Gurbani the rahao marks a hymn's central theme.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the song hook repeated day 533's round-song hook; replaced with a book-title image. The claim that the whole bani 'unfolds out of' the rahao is now offered as one way to read it, and the hook and myth say only what the line shows (the bani's name comes from it).

The outline attributes 'sukhmanee sukh amrit prabh naam' to ashtpadi 24; the writer understands it as the rahao near the beginning (Ang 262) and wrote the day that way. A Keeper should confirm, and say if the line also recurs in ashtpadi 24.
Paraphrase of the rahao (sukhmanee sukh amrit prabh naam; bhagat janaa kai man bisraam): confirm.
Readings of the title (jewel of peace / peace of mind) are given without ranking.
